title: Classes in depth
lesson:
In Level 1 you wrote methods, and then a class or two: an `Enemy` with a `Health` property, an `Inventory` with a dictionary inside. A class bundles **data** (fields and properties) with the **methods** that are allowed to change it. Level 2 is about doing that well, because in a real game or app most bugs come from data being changed by the wrong code at the wrong time.

**The constructor sets the object up properly, or refuses.** If a water tank with capacity 0 makes no sense, don't allow one to exist:

```
public WaterTank(double capacity)
{
    if (capacity <= 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(capacity));
    Capacity = capacity;
}
```

Now every `WaterTank` in your program is valid. You never have to check it again.

**Properties control who can change what.**
- `public double Capacity { get; }` can only be set in the constructor.
- `public double Level { get; private set; }` can be read by anyone but changed only by the tank's own methods (`Fill`, `Draw`), which keep the rules.
- `public string Name { get; init; }` can be set once, in an object initializer (`new Profile { Name = "Amina" }`), then never again.
- A property with a body can **validate**: `set => volume = Math.Clamp(value, 0, 100);` means no caller can ever store 150.

This is **encapsulation**: the class protects its own rules. The common mistake is making everything `public { get; set; }` "to be easy". Then any line anywhere can write `tank.Level = -40`, and you spend an evening hunting the line that did it.

**Static members belong to the class, not to one object.** `static int Issued` is one counter shared by every ticket. Use static for things that really are shared (a count, a factory method, a helper like `Math.Max`). Be careful: static state lives for the whole program, so tests have to reset it.

In Unity you'll see the same shape: `[SerializeField] private int maxHealth;` shows a private field in the editor, and a public read-only property lets other scripts look without touching.

notes: The constructor throws for a bad capacity, so an invalid tank can never exist.
Level has a private setter: only Fill (and other tank methods) can change it.
PercentFull is a computed property: it has no storage, it's worked out each time.
Name uses init: set in the object initializer, then fixed.
Volume's setter clamps, so 150 is stored as 100.
Created is static: one counter for the whole class.

exercises.title: A water tank
exercises.prompt:
Write class WaterTank:
- constructor WaterTank(double capacity): throw ArgumentOutOfRangeException if capacity is 0 or less.
- property Capacity (get only) and Level (get; private set;), starting at 0.
- PercentFull: Level / Capacity * 100, rounded to 1 decimal.
- double Fill(double litres): adds what fits, returns how much spilled over. Negative litres: ArgumentOutOfRangeException.
- double Draw(double litres): takes out up to that much, returns what was really drawn. Negative litres: ArgumentOutOfRangeException.

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var t = new WaterTank(1000); double spill = t.Fill(1200); return t.Level + " " + spill + " " + t.PercentFull; }))()
tests.name: fill past the top

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var t = new WaterTank(500); t.Fill(200); double got = t.Draw(50); return t.Level + " " + got + " " + t.PercentFull; }))()
tests.name: fill and draw

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var t = new WaterTank(300); t.Fill(100); return t.Draw(250) + " " + t.Level; }))()
tests.name: draw more than there is
tests.hint_if_fail: Draw can only give what is in the tank: Math.Min(Level, litres).

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var t = new WaterTank(100); t.Fill(-5); return "no error"; }))()
tests.name: negative fill is refused

tests.why: Level should have a private setter so only the tank can change it.

hints: Start with the guard in the constructor: if (capacity <= 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(capacity));
Fill: double added = Math.Min(Capacity - Level, litres); Level += added; return litres - added;
Draw: double taken = Math.Min(Level, litres); Level -= taken; return taken;

exercises.title: A player profile
exercises.prompt:
Write class PlayerProfile:
- Name: get and init. Default "Player". The init accessor trims the value and throws ArgumentException if it is null or blank.
- Volume: get and set, default 80. The setter clamps to 0..100 (150 becomes 100, -3 becomes 0).
- Xp: get; private set; starts at 0. void AddXp(int amount) adds to it; a negative amount throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException.
- Level: computed, Xp / 100 + 1 (so 250 xp is level 3).

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var p = new PlayerProfile { Name = "Juma" }; p.Volume = 150; int a = p.Volume; p.Volume = -3; return a + " " + p.Volume; }))()
tests.name: volume is clamped

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var p = new PlayerProfile(); p.AddXp(250); return p.Xp + " " + p.Level; }))()
tests.name: xp and level

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var p = new PlayerProfile(); p.AddXp(-10); return "no error"; }))()
tests.name: negative xp is refused

tests.why: Name should use an init accessor.

hints: Name needs a backing field: private readonly string name = "Player"; then get => name; init { ... name = value.Trim(); }
Volume: private int volume = 80; public int Volume { get => volume; set => volume = Math.Clamp(value, 0, 100); }
Level doesn't need storage: public int Level => Xp / 100 + 1;

exercises.title: Clinic tickets (static members)
exercises.prompt:
Write class Ticket for a clinic queue:
- static int Issued { get; private set; }: how many tickets were made today.
- constructor Ticket(string patient): throws ArgumentException if the name is null or blank; stores the trimmed name in Patient; adds 1 to Issued and uses it as this ticket's Number (first ticket is 1).
- static void ResetDay(): sets Issued back to 0.
- static string NextUp(int served): "Queue empty" if served >= Issued, otherwise "Now serving #N" where N = served + 1.
- ToString(): "#2 Juma".

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { Ticket.ResetDay(); var a = new Ticket("Amina"); var b = new Ticket("Juma"); return a + ", " + b + " | " + Ticket.Issued; }))()
tests.name: numbers count up

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { Ticket.ResetDay(); new Ticket("A"); new Ticket("B"); new Ticket("C"); return Ticket.NextUp(1); }))()
tests.name: next up

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { Ticket.ResetDay(); new Ticket("A"); Ticket.ResetDay(); return new Ticket(" Otieno ").ToString(); }))()
tests.name: reset starts again at 1

hints: public static int Issued { get; private set; } is shared by every ticket.
In the constructor: check the name, then Issued++; Number = Issued;
public static string NextUp(int served) => served >= Issued ? "Queue empty" : $"Now serving #{served + 1}";

quiz.q: Why throw an exception in the constructor for a capacity of 0?
choices: So an invalid object can never exist, and no other code has to check
quiz.why: Guard the door once; every object after that is valid.

quiz.q: public double Level { get; private set; } means…
choices: anyone can read it; only the class's own code can change it
it can be set once in an initializer

quiz.q: What does an init accessor allow?
choices: Setting it only in the constructor or an object initializer, then never again

quiz.q: Ticket.Issued is static. If you make 3 tickets, how many Issued counters exist?
quiz.why: Static members belong to the class.

quiz.q: A teammate makes every property public { get; set; } 'to keep it simple'. What is the real risk?
choices: Any code anywhere can break the object's rules, and bugs become hard to trace
quiz.why: Encapsulation keeps the rules in one place.

cards.a: public int X { get; private set; }
Belongs to the class, shared by all objects: Ticket.Issued

explain: Explain encapsulation in your own words, using an example you make up (a fuel tank, a bank account, a game character).
